extracted_claims.text: Article 43 provides two conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: an internal control procedure (Annex VI, self-assessment) or an assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body (Annex VII).

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric identification), the provider may use internal control or an assessment involving a notified body, with the choice depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Section A of Annex I (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies additionally verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements.

The provider may choose any notified body for the Annex VII procedure, except that where the system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or Union institutions/bodies, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body.
A substantially modified high-risk AI system must undergo a new conformity assessment, unless the modification was predetermined by the provider as part of continuous learning.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, to authorise placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems for limited, exceptional reasons (public security, health, environment, key infrastructure) for a limited period.
Article 35 of the AI Act establishes the system of identification numbers and lists of notified bodies.

Annex VII permits a notified body, where other reasonable means of verifying conformity have proven insufficient and upon reasoned request, to be granted access to training and trained models of the AI system, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards.

Article 44 governs certificates issued by notified bodies and Article 45 sets information obligations of notified bodies, within Section 5 of the AI Act (Articles 40-49) covering standards, conformity assessment, certificates and registration.

A European Commission proposal, COM(2025) 836, would create a new Annex XIV listing codes/categories of AI systems for the Commission's NANDO information system to support notified-body designation under the AI Act; this is a proposed amendment, not yet adopted law.

A Council document (ST-7322-2026) lists proposed codes and categories (e.g., AIP 0101-0105) setting the scope of designation of conformity assessment bodies, referencing 'Article 30' of the Regulation as the legal basis for designation.
As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act in the context of medical devices/MDR-IVDR interplay.

A 2025-published source states that AI Act-specific conformity assessments by designated notified bodies will only begin after the high-risk obligations deadline, implying none were operating at time of publication.
High-risk AI system obligations under the AI Act, including conformity assessment requirements, are stated to fully apply from August 2026 (with some sources citing August 2, 2026 specifically).
As of October 2025, the NANDO database listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies; this figure concerns medical device legislation (MDR/IVDR), not AI Act-specific designations.

As of late June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) in the NANDO database; the CRA is a separate regulation from the AI Act, with its rules on notified bodies applying from 11 June 2026 and full application from 11 December 2027.

The November 2022 proposal version of Article 43 applied the notified-body/harmonised-standards framework specifically and only to high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, differing in scope from the finally adopted Article 43.

A commercial blog post asserts that every high-risk AI system needs an 'algorithm passport' registered with the AI Office before first use, framed as a legal requirement; no official EU source (Articles 43-49, Annexes VI/VII) corroborates this requirement.

contradictions.claim_a: The Council document ST-7322-2026 references 'Article 30' of the Regulation as setting the scope for designation of conformity assessment bodies.
contradictions.claim_b: Other EU guidance sources identify Article 35 as governing identification numbers and lists of notified bodies, and Articles 43-45 as governing the conformity assessment procedure and notified body obligations, without reference to an Article 30 basis for designation scope.
contradictions.description: Source 8 cites 'Article 30' as the basis for the scope of notified body designation under the AI Act, while other official/guidance sources (11-13, 24) describe the relevant provisions as Articles 35, 43-45, creating an unresolved discrepancy in article numbering/legal basis.

contradictions.claim_a: The 2022 proposal text of Article 43 limited the notified-body/harmonised-standards conformity assessment framework specifically to high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III.
contradictions.claim_b: The finalized/adopted Article 43 extends conformity assessment requirements more broadly, including systems under Annex I Section A (sectoral product legislation) and other Annex III points (2-8), with differentiated procedures.
contradictions.description: The 2022 proposal version of Article 43 described a narrower scope than the finally adopted version, reflecting legislative changes between proposal and adoption; summaries should not conflate the two as the same current law.

contradictions.claim_a: As of March-April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act (sources 21, 22).
contradictions.claim_b: Figures reported for MDR/IVDR notified bodies (51 and 19 respectively, as of October 2025) might be mistakenly read as applicable to AI Act designations, though they concern a different, pre-existing medical-device regulatory framework.
contradictions.description: There is a risk of conflating the well-established MDR/IVDR notified body counts (source 7) with AI Act-specific notified body designations, which multiple 2026 sources confirm had not yet occurred (sources 21, 22).

open_issues: No official EU source in this set confirms that any notified bodies have been formally designated specifically under the AI Act as of the current date (October 2026); the most recent sources only cover up to around June 2026 and report zero or unclear designations.

The exact relationship between the proposed COM(2025) 836 amendment (new Annex XIV / NANDO integration) and the existing Article 35 notified-body listing mechanism is not clarified — it is unclear whether this proposal has been adopted or remains pending.

The legal basis cited in the Council document (Article 30) for the scope of conformity assessment body designation is inconsistent with other sources' references to Articles 35 and 43-45; sources do not resolve this numbering discrepancy.

Sources do not clarify whether existing MDR/IVDR-designated notified bodies will automatically gain AI Act designation for Annex I Section A high-risk AI systems, or whether a separate AI Act-specific designation process is required.

The claim about an 'algorithm passport' requirement registered with the 'AI Office' appears in only one promotional/blog source and is not corroborated by any official AI Act text or guidance; its legal accuracy could not be verified from the provided sources.

Sources do not specify current (post-June 2026) counts or identities of any notified bodies designated under the AI Act, leaving the real-world state of conformity assessment infrastructure as of October 2026 unresolved.

The interaction between the Cyber Resilience Act's notified body regime (source 20) and the AI Act's own regime is not addressed by any source, leaving open whether manufacturers of overlapping products face parallel or unified assessment requirements.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main routes for conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems: internal control (self-assessment) and third-party assessment by a notified body, with the applicable route depending on the system's category (low confidence). However, available evidence suggests that as of mid-2026, the notified-body ecosystem specifically for the AI Act remained largely undeveloped, with no confirmed designations identified in the sources reviewed (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 provides two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: an internal control procedure under Annex VI (self-assessment), or an assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) [powerquant.eu](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment). For high-risk systems under point 1 of Annex III, such as biometric identification, providers may choose internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai).

For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Annex I, Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai).

Providers may generally choose any notified body for the Annex VII procedure, except where systems are intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43). A substantially modified high-risk system requires a new conformity assessment, unless the modification was predetermined as part of continuous learning (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43). Article 46 permits a market surveillance authority, by derogation, to authorise placing a specific high-risk system on the market for limited, exceptional reasons (public security, health, environment, key infrastructure) for a limited time (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46). Annex VII also allows notified bodies, upon reasoned request, to access training data and trained models when other verification means are insufficient, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7).

### Notified Body Designation Framework
Article 35 establishes the system of identification numbers and lists of notified bodies (low confidence) [regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35). Articles 44-45 govern certificates issued by notified bodies and their information obligations (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-60). A Commission proposal, COM(2025) 836, would create a new Annex XIV listing AI system codes/categories for the NANDO database to support notified-body designation—this remains a proposal, not adopted law (medium confidence) [Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf). A related Council document lists proposed designation codes (e.g., AIP 0101-0105), though it cites "Article 30" as the legal basis, which conflicts with other sources referencing Articles 35 and 43-45 (medium confidence) [Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf).

### Current State of Designations
As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies, but this concerns medical device legislation, not AI Act-specific designations (high confidence) [EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051). As of March 2026, the AI Act notified body ecosystem was still being built, with designation processes ongoing and limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline (low confidence) [eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act). As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated in the context of medical device/MDR-IVDR interplay (low confidence) [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide). High-risk obligations, including conformity assessment, are generally stated to apply from August 2, 2026 (low confidence) [mdxcro.com](https://mdxcro.com/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-samd), [sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the legal basis for designation scope: one Council document cites "Article 30" while others reference Articles 35 and 43-45 (both low/medium confidence, unresolved). The core claim that Article 43 provides two conformity assessment routes is itself rated low confidence (0.17-0.24) despite broad corroboration, reflecting low source authority; readers should treat it as a widely repeated interpretation rather than a directly verified legal citation. The 2022 proposal text of Article 43 had a narrower scope than the finally adopted version—older summaries should not be conflated with current law (low confidence). MDR/IVDR notified body counts should not be confused with AI Act-specific designations, which multiple 2026 sources suggest had not yet materialized. A claim about a mandatory "algorithm passport" registered with the AI Office appears in only one promotional source and is uncorroborated by official texts (low confidence, flagged as unreliable).

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms formal AI Act notified-body designations as of the most recent data (mid-2026). The relationship between COM(2025) 836's proposed Annex XIV/NANDO mechanism and existing Article 35 processes is unclear, and its adoption status is unconfirmed. Whether MDR/IVDR-designated bodies automatically gain AI Act authority, or need separate designation, is unaddressed. The interaction between AI Act and Cyber Resilience Act notified-body regimes for overlapping products is unexplored.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main routes for conformity assessment of high-risk AI systems: internal control (self-assessment) and third-party assessment by a notified body, with the applicable route depending on the system's category (medium confidence). However, available evidence suggests that as of mid-2026, the notified-body ecosystem specifically for the AI Act remained largely undeveloped, with no confirmed designations identified in the sources reviewed (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 provides two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: an internal control procedure under Annex VI (self-assessment), or an assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) [powerquant.eu](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment). For high-risk systems under point 1 of Annex III, such as biometric identification, providers may choose internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai).

For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Annex I, Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai).

Providers may generally choose any notified body for the Annex VII procedure, except where systems are intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43). A substantially modified high-risk system requires a new conformity assessment, unless the modification was predetermined as part of continuous learning (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43). Article 46 permits a market surveillance authority, by derogation, to authorise placing a specific high-risk system on the market for limited, exceptional reasons (public security, health, environment, key infrastructure) for a limited time (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46). Annex VII also allows notified bodies, upon reasoned request, to access training data and trained models when other verification means are insufficient, subject to IP and confidentiality safeguards (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7).

### Notified Body Designation Framework
Article 35 establishes the system of identification numbers and lists of notified bodies (low confidence) [regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/articles/article-35). Articles 44-45 govern certificates issued by notified bodies and their information obligations (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-60). A Commission proposal, COM(2025) 836, would create a new Annex XIV listing AI system codes/categories for the NANDO database to support notified-body designation—this remains a proposal, not adopted law (medium confidence) [Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf). A related Council document lists proposed designation codes (e.g., AIP 0101-0105), though it cites "Article 30" as the legal basis, which conflicts with other sources referencing Articles 35 and 43-45 (medium confidence) [Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf).

### Current State of Designations
As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies, but this concerns medical device legislation, not AI Act-specific designations (high confidence) [EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051). As of March 2026, the AI Act notified body ecosystem was still being built, with designation processes ongoing and limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline (low confidence) [eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act). As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated in the context of medical device/MDR-IVDR interplay (low confidence) [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide). High-risk obligations, including conformity assessment, are generally stated to apply from August 2, 2026 (low confidence) [mdxcro.com](https://mdxcro.com/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-samd), [sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on the legal basis for designation scope: one Council document cites "Article 30" while others reference Articles 35 and 43-45 (both low/medium confidence, unresolved). The 2022 proposal text of Article 43 had a narrower scope than the finally adopted version—older summaries should not be conflated with current law (low confidence). MDR/IVDR notified body counts should not be confused with AI Act-specific designations, which multiple 2026 sources suggest had not yet materialized. A claim about a mandatory "algorithm passport" registered with the AI Office appears in only one promotional source and is uncorroborated by official texts (low confidence, flagged as unreliable).

## Knowledge Gaps
No source confirms formal AI Act notified-body designations as of the most recent data (mid-2026). The relationship between COM(2025) 836's proposed Annex XIV/NANDO mechanism and existing Article 35 processes is unclear, and its adoption status is unconfirmed. Whether MDR/IVDR-designated bodies automatically gain AI Act authority, or need separate designation, is unaddressed. The interaction between AI Act and Cyber Resilience Act notified-body regimes for overlapping products is unexplored.
